messages.subject: Interpret Data From NBA Model
parts:
The goal is to model NBA team tendencies to perform well or poorly in a given quarter. 

The most basic model to predict outcomes in a quarter is a linear regression where the margin of victory for a given quarter is predicted by the publicly available Vegas full game spread.  So for instance, if the Spurs are playing the 76ers and Vegas says Spurs win the game by 14 pts, a regression equation ignoring team tendencies would predicts that Spurs win second quarter by about 4 points.  This works OKAY.  I'm hypothesizing that I can predict quarter outcomes better by including specific team tendencies.  Spurs have a particularly great bench so maybe they outperform in the 2nd quarter.

I use this code.  It's in JAGS but I think its basically the same as STAN and okay to post right? The variable line is equal to the vegas line.  And I set the beta1[j] prior very high because I don't see any reason why the relation between full game line and quarter performance would change based on the team.  I do think the y intercept my change though...

model {
  for (i in 1:Ntotal) {
    y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1 / (sigma ^ 2))
    mu[i] <- beta0[team[i]] + beta1[team[i]] * line[i]
  }

  for (j in 1:Nsubj) {
    beta0[j] ~ dnorm( beta0mu, 1)
    beta1[j] ~ dnorm( beta1mu, 1000)
  }
 
  beta0mu  ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01)
  beta1mu  ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01 )
  sigma ~ dunif( 0.01, 100 )
}"

parts:
> On Feb 28, 2016, at 10:53 PM, Daniel Ashman <dmaxa...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> The goal is to model NBA team tendencies to perform well or poorly in a given quarter.
>
> The most basic model to predict outcomes in a quarter is a linear regression where the margin of victory for a given quarter is predicted by the publicly available Vegas full game spread. So for instance, if the Spurs are playing the 76ers and Vegas says Spurs win the game by 14 pts, a regression equation ignoring team tendencies would predicts that Spurs win second quarter by about 4 points. This works OKAY. I'm hypothesizing that I can predict quarter outcomes better by including specific team tendencies. Spurs have a particularly great bench so maybe they outperform in the 2nd quarter.
>
> I use this code. It's in JAGS but I think its basically the same as STAN and okay to post right? The variable line is equal to the vegas line. And I set the beta1[j] prior very high because I don't see any reason why the relation between full game line and quarter performance would change based on the team. I do think the y intercept my change though...
>
> model {
> for (i in 1:Ntotal) {
> y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1 / (sigma ^ 2))
> mu[i] <- beta0[team[i]] + beta1[team[i]] * line[i]
> }
>
> for (j in 1:Nsubj) {
> beta0[j] ~ dnorm( beta0mu, 1)
> beta1[j] ~ dnorm( beta1mu, 1000)
> }
>
> beta0mu ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01)
> beta1mu ~ dnorm( 0, 0.01 )
> sigma ~ dunif( 0.01, 100 )
> }"

That 1000 is an awfully tight prior in JAGS/BUGS.

The Stan model's fully vectorizable.

model {
y ~ normal(beta0[team] + beta1[team] .* line, sigma);
beta0 ~ normal(beta0mu, 1);
beta1 ~ normal(beta1mu, .03);
beta0mu ~ normal(0, 10);
beta1mu ~ normal(0, 10);
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

}

>
> Here are the results for beta[0] (where each beta[j] represents a different teams performance in the 2nd quarter.

We'd probably fit a hierarchical model of the regression coefficients
varying by quarter, probably with a multivariate normal hierarchical
prior. What you're doing in fitting separate models to each quarter
is what Andrew calls "the secret weapon" (for
reasons that escape me, as it seems the obvious thing to do if
you can't or don't want to formulate a joint model).

All of these terms are loaded statistical baggage.

What you have in Bayesian terms is a posterior probability
that the team's going to overperform or underperform, with
an estimate of the performance and uncertainty intervals.
The model estimates a 97.5% chance or so that team 24 is
overperforming and also a 75%+ chance team 23 is underperforming.

You can calculate these in Stan as generated quantities as follows:

generated quantities {
int<lower=0, upper=1> overperform[30];
for (n in 1:30)
overperform[n] <- (beta0[n] > 0);
}

Then the posterior mean of overperform[n] is the posterior estimate
(based on model and observed data) that team overperforms in the quarter.

> Is this a sound interpretation? What about teams 23 and 24, they seem to have statistically significant tendencies here, should I assume the mean for those two teams is correct? Any thoughts or questions are welcome! Thanks!

We don't tend to think in terms of statistical significance.
Instead, we might compare two models predictively, one in
which the performance is allowed to vary by quarter and one in
which it isn't. And then do tests on how well these match the
in-sample or held-out data.

- Bob
